column4: The measured rain fills valleys according to their capacity, flood and smelting produce foam, the scum passes, and what benefits people remains; one ayah therefore gathers the section's measure, pasture-debris, fire, benefit, and permanence.
Moses sees a fire from afar and approaches hoping for a brand or guidance at it, the exact meeting through which the section turns threatening fire into a road.
At the fire God says that He has chosen Moses and commands him to listen, grounding the section's claim that selection is the first gift at this fire.
The fire-side revelation commands Moses to worship God and establish prayer for His remembrance, directly joining the section's prayer and remembering scenes.
The coming Hour is almost kept hidden so every soul may be repaid for its striving; this is the hidden reality the section places after prayer at the fire.
When Moses reaches the fire, blessing is announced around it and God is glorified as Lord of the worlds; the fire scene thus actually voices the section's opening glorification.
The magicians are cast down in prostration and declare faith, beginning the communal choice that the section reads beside purification and prayer.
Pharaoh threatens the believing magicians and claims that his punishment is more severe and more enduring, supplying the false claim to permanence that their answer overturns.
The magicians refuse to prefer Pharaoh over the clear proofs and say that he can decree only in this worldly life, directly joining preference, allotted judgment, and the lower life.
The magicians seek forgiveness and answer Pharaoh that God is better and more enduring, the precise confession heard again in the section's contrast between the present life and what lasts.
The criminal comes to Hell and there neither dies nor lives, exactly supplying the condition named in the section's fire sequence.
The believer who does righteous deeds receives the highest degrees, meeting the section's language of height within the same magician passage.
Gardens and abiding reward are called the recompense of one who purifies himself, completing the section's movement from purification to lasting life.
The flower of worldly life is a temporary trial while the Lord's provision is better and more enduring, directly merging pasture, provision, preference, and permanence.
Worldly life is likened to rain-grown vegetation that becomes dry fragments scattered by wind, the section's explicit meeting of the preferred lower life with spent pasture.
Immediately after the dried vegetation, enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope; this ayah supplies the lasting selection on the other side of 18:45.
One ayah moves from embryo stages and what is formed or unformed in wombs to dead earth stirring and growing after rain, exactly joining fashioned body to pasture.
The drop becomes a clot and God then creates and proportions it, using the creation-and-fashioning pair in the embryonic sense developed by the section.
Abraham asks his Lord to keep him and his children away from worshipping idols, the specific Abrahamic prayer the section hears behind the first scrolls and avoidance.
Cultivated gardens and crops grow, their fruit is eaten, and their due is given on harvest day; this is the worked field and paid right set against abandoned grass.
The ayah distinguishes the crop of the Hereafter, which is increased, from the crop of this world, which leaves no share in the Hereafter, making the section's two fields explicit.
Worldly goods are temporary adornment, while what is with God is better and more enduring, a direct restatement of the section's decisive choice.
What people receive is enjoyment of worldly life, while what is with God is better and more enduring for trusting believers, repeating the section's scale of value.
Moses reaches the fire and is called by name; this row contributes the actual arrival and call between the sight in 20:10 and the selection in 20:13.
At the fire Moses learns that the caller is his Lord and that he stands in the sacred valley of Tuwa, fixing the section's meeting in its revealed place.
Moses tells his family that he has perceived a fire and may return with news or a burning brand, the alternate opening of the section's fire-and-guidance scene.
After the glorification at the fire, the speaker identifies Himself to Moses as God, the Mighty and Wise; it completes whose voice turns the fire into guidance.
After completing his term, Moses sees a fire from the side of the mount and seeks news or a brand so his family may warm themselves, repeating the journey toward a useful fire.
When Moses reaches that fire, he is called from the blessed tract and told that the speaker is God, Lord of the worlds, completing the alternate fire revelation.
God recounts Moses' rescues and says that he came at an appointed measure, bringing divine measure into the very life that later reaches the fire.
God says that He fashioned or chose Moses for Himself, reinforcing the section's meeting between skilled formation and divine selection.
Moses and Aaron are sent with God's signs and told not to slacken in His remembrance, extending the fire-side command into their mission.
They must speak gently to Pharaoh so that he may remember or fear, directly anticipating the section's person who takes reminder through fear.
Moses describes the Lord as the One who gave everything its created form and then guided it, a compact parallel to creating, fashioning, measuring, and guiding.
Immediately after the worldly flower, the Prophet is told to command his household to prayer and persist, while God provides; this joins prayer to the better provision of 20:131.
In the same passage, the proof is said already to have come in the former scriptures, directly meeting the section's closing appeal to the earliest scrolls.
The listener is asked whether he was informed of what is in the scrolls of Moses, an independent Quranic witness to the section's closing scriptural memory.
Abraham who fulfilled is named beside Moses' scrolls, completing the same pairing of Abraham and Moses that closes the section.
In another telling, the magicians are cast down in prostration, directly repeating the bodily act through which the section's group makes its choice.
The prostrate magicians declare faith in the Lord of the worlds, linking their response to the same divine title glorified at Moses' fire.
They identify that Lord as the Lord of Moses and Aaron, fixing the confession in the same Musa narrative rather than as a generic prostration.
Pharaoh objects that they believed before his permission and accuses them of conspiracy, repeating the worldly ruler's attempt to own their choice.
Pharaoh threatens mutilation and crucifixion, giving the temporal punishment against which the magicians choose the Lord's lasting judgment.
The magicians answer that they are returning to their Lord, stating why Pharaoh's worldly threat cannot be the enduring end.
They ask for patience and to die in submission because their only offense was belief in the signs, resolving the threatened death through faithful prayer.
A further account again has the magicians thrown down in prostration, confirming the section's central posture across the repeated scene.
The prostrate magicians say that they believe in the Lord of the worlds, contributing their confession to the repeated scene.
They specify the Lord of Moses and Aaron, tying that confession to Moses' mission.
Pharaoh again denies their right to believe without his permission and threatens bodily punishment, repeating his claim over choice and life.
The magicians answer that the threat does no harm because they will return to their Lord, making their preference for the lasting destination explicit.
They hope for their Lord's forgiveness because they were first to believe, showing what the section's chosen turn at the scene seeks.
Moses asks Pharaoh whether he is willing to purify himself, placing purification at the center of another Musa encounter.
Moses offers to guide Pharaoh to his Lord so that he will fear, directly joining guidance to the fear that makes reminder effective.
Pharaoh claims to be the highest lord; the claim is the explicit human usurpation of the section's opening name, the Lord Most High.
Pharaoh's fate is called a lesson for one who fears, connecting the Musa narrative itself to the section's fear-responsive reminder.
God brings the earth's water and pasture out of it, restaging the provision that later dries and passes.
Hell is made visible to whoever sees, turning the once-hidden destination into the manifest fire before the human choice is judged.
The next division begins with the one who transgressed, identifying the person whose preference leads to the fire named around it.
That person prefers worldly life, using the section's exact act of preference in the same eschatological division.
Hell is then his refuge, directly joining preference for the lower life to entry into fire.
The opposite person fears standing before his Lord and restrains desire, stating the fear-led choice on the other branch.
The Garden becomes that person's refuge, completing the alternative to the fire across the section's two human responses.
The Prophet is only a warner to the one who fears the Hour, closely matching the command to remind and the one who will remember through fear.
The soul and the One who proportioned it extend the section's craft of bodily fashioning into moral formation.
The fashioned soul is shown its corruption and its piety, supplying the two possibilities that make purification a choice.
Prosperity belongs to the one who purifies the soul, the closest Quranic counterpart to the section's pairing of falah and tazakka.
Failure belongs to the one who buries or stunts the soul, the cultivated-field reversal of purification and growth.
God declares that guidance belongs to Him, matching the section's guided road and the Lord who guides what He forms.
The Hereafter and the first life belong to God, setting the two temporal sides before the warning of fire.
God warns of a blazing fire, the same warning to which the section's people respond in opposite ways.
Only the most wretched enters that fire, an especially close parallel to the section's wretched person who burns in the greater fire.
The most wretched is identified as the one who denied and turned away, explaining his rejection of reminder.
The God-fearing person is kept away from the fire, reversing the wretched person's approach and echoing avoidance in the section.
He gives his wealth in order to purify himself, giving concrete action to the purification on the saved branch.
His aim is the face of his Lord, the Most High, bringing purification under the same divine name that opens the section.
God asks why people do not affirm the One who created them, opening a sustained creation-field-fire sequence that closely matches the section's meetings.
The ayah asks whether humans create the emitted seed or God is its creator, making bodily creation the first scene in that sequence.
God says that He has measured death among people, joining bodily destiny to the section's measuring and its boundary between death and life.
The listener is asked to consider what he tills, directly staging the worked field behind the section's agricultural sense of falah.
God asks whether people make the crop grow or He does, attributing the field's useful growth to the Creator.
God could make the crop shattered dry debris, the direct reversal of growth and counterpart to the spent pasture.
The listener is next asked to consider the water he drinks, opening the water scene that feeds the field.
God asks whether people send that water down from the raincloud or He does, locating provision in the descending water.
God could make the water bitter, marking the boundary between offered provision and unusable water.
The listener is then asked to consider the fire he kindles, moving the same sequence from water and field to fire.
God asks whether people produced the fire's tree or He did, joining vegetation, creative craft, and kindled fire.
God made that fire a reminder and a provision for travelers, the clearest parallel to the section's fire that guides rather than consumes.
The creation, crop, water, and fire sequence ends by commanding glorification of the name of the mighty Lord, closely matching the section's opening command.
God produces fire for people from the green tree, so vegetation and fire meet in one object as they do across the section.
Water is sent from the sky in due measure, lodged in the earth, and remains subject to removal, a close parallel to measured water and what stays or disappears.
A destroyed people are made ghutha, debris swept away; the pasture word becomes a human fate and sharpens the section's image of what does not remain.
Rain becomes springs and many-colored crops, then withers yellow and turns to debris, and the whole scene is explicitly a reminder for understanding people.
Worldly life is illustrated by rain-grown vegetation that delights cultivators, then yellows and becomes debris before the lasting judgment, joining pasture to preference.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, stating in bare form the section's distinction between passing scum and lasting benefit.
Whoever chooses the immediate life receives a measured portion and then reaches Hell, joining preference, allotment, and fire.
Whoever chooses the Hereafter and strives for it in faith has that striving appreciated, completing the opposite branch of the choice.
God's worldly preferences between people are surpassed by the Hereafter's greater degrees and greater preference, joining allotment, selection, and height.
Those who fear their Lord unseen and establish prayer can receive the warning, and whoever purifies does so for himself; the ayah gathers fear, prayer, hiddenness, and purification.
The people of the Fire are neither finished by death nor relieved of punishment, a direct parallel to the section's life suspended between death and life.
The condemned person has death coming from every side yet does not die, another precise Quranic rendering of the section's impossible state in fire.
God forms people in the wombs however He wills, directly joining bodily fashioning to divine choice.
God knows every pregnancy and what wombs diminish or increase, and everything with Him has a measure; womb, hidden knowledge, and measure meet in one ayah.
Knowledge of the Hour, descending rain, and what is in wombs belongs to God, collecting the section's hidden Hour, pasture-making water, and formed body.
Knowledge of the Hour returns to God, and no fruit emerges or female conceives and gives birth outside His knowledge, linking hidden time, crop, and womb.
God creates the human from a drop and measures him, joining bodily origin to determination.
God then eases the human's way, directly pairing measured formation with the eased path promised in the section.
God is the One who created, proportioned, and balanced the human, a direct bodily use of the section's craft vocabulary.
God creates everything and determines it with exact determination, stating together the two divine acts that organize the section.
Everything is created according to measure, the universal formulation behind the measured valley, body, and human share.
God's treasuries are inexhaustible, but He sends each thing down only in a known measure, clarifying measured provision from what remains hidden.
Water descends from heaven in measure, revives dead land, and becomes an image of human emergence, linking pasture, measure, and bodily return.
The humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends, and its revival proves that its Giver revives the dead, paralleling the womb-to-field movement.
Water is driven to barren land and brings forth crops eaten by people and cattle, directly staging pasture as measured provision.
The Prophet is commanded to remind because reminder benefits believers, making explicit the benefit condition attached to reminder in the section.
The Prophet is told to remind with the Quran whoever fears the warning, directly matching reminder addressed to fear.
Warning reaches the one who follows the Reminder and fears the Merciful unseen, combining receptive remembrance, fear, and hiddenness.
The revelation is itself called a reminder, beginning a short passage that joins willing remembrance to elevated purified scrolls.
Whoever wills may remember it, making the hearer's choice part of the reminder scene.
That reminder is in honored scrolls, directly meeting the section's close in the earlier scrolls.
The scrolls are raised and purified, joining the section's height and purification within its scriptural image.
God's messenger recites purified scrolls, bringing recitation and purification into the same written object recalled at the section's close.
Those scrolls contain upright writings, specifying the enduring content carried by the purified pages.
The Quran is a reminder to all worlds, establishing the offered reminder before the following choice of path.
The reminder is for whoever wills to take a straight way, joining recollection, choice, and path.
Human willing remains under the will of God, Lord of the worlds, matching the section's exception for what God wills.
The Prophet is commanded to remember the name of his Lord and devote himself wholly to Him, closely paralleling remembering the Lord's name before prayer.
The Prophet is commanded to recite revelation and establish prayer, and God's remembrance is declared greater; recitation, prayer, and remembrance meet explicitly.
After prayer people seek God's bounty and remember Him much so that they may prosper, joining provision, remembrance, and falah.
Charity purifies and develops believers, and the Prophet is told to pray for them, placing purification and prayer in one command.
Abraham settles his family in an uncultivated valley so they may establish prayer and asks that they receive fruits, joining barren land, prayer, inclination, and provision.
Within Abraham's prayer, God knows what people conceal and disclose, echoing the section's divine knowledge of hidden and open things.
Abraham asks to be made an establisher of prayer together with his descendants, completing the prayer behind the section's mention of his pages.
Moses and Aaron receive the Criterion, light, and a reminder for the God-fearing, joining Musa's scripture to guidance and remembrance.
Those recipients fear their Lord unseen and dread the Hour, defining the fear that receives the Mosaic reminder.
The Lord creates what He wills and chooses, while creatures do not own the choice; creation and selection meet in one divine act.
Moses is described as chosen and as a messenger-prophet, confirming chosenness as a defining feature of his encounter.
God calls Moses from the right side of the mount and brings him near for intimate speech, another concise version of approach becoming revelation.
God tells Moses that He chose him over people through His messages and speech, an explicit counterpart to the fire-side selection.
Humanity is created in the finest form, supplying the well-fashioned body in the section's craft image.
The well-formed human is then returned to the lowest of the low, a stark descent from fashioned height that illuminates the lower-life image.
Faith and good works receive an unending reward, completing the reversal from the lowest condition to what endures.
Immediately before the magicians prostrate, the magician is said not to prosper wherever he comes; their purification scene crosses from failed magic to the falah of the purified.
Seeking a divided share by divining arrows is forbidden, providing a concrete boundary for the section's carved shaft and its movement from allotment to chosen share.
Divining arrows are classed with abominations to be avoided so that people may prosper, opposing illicit selection by lots to true falah.
The people of Saqar are asked what brought them into the fire, opening an explicit fire-versus-prayer explanation.
They answer that they were not among those who prayed, making neglected prayer the boundary opposite the section's person who remembers and prays.
A kindled fire briefly gives light, but God removes the light and leaves its people in darkness; it reverses Moses' fire, which yields guidance rather than lost sight.
Worldly life is rain-mixed vegetation that flourishes and is suddenly made a reaped field, a specific parallel to the pasture whose apparent life passes.
The believer in Pharaoh's court calls worldly life brief enjoyment and the Hereafter the enduring home, restating the magician scene's scale in another Pharaonic speech.
Worldly life is play and diversion while the Home of the Hereafter is the true life, clarifying the section's lower life and its state that is neither death nor real life.
People are said to love the immediate life, a close nonlexical parallel to preferring the nearer worldly life.
They leave the Hereafter aside, completing the two-sided preference begun in 75:20.
People love the immediate life and leave behind a weighty Day, again linking preference to neglect of the lasting reckoning.
Those who prefer worldly life over the Hereafter also obstruct God's path, joining bad preference to loss of the guided road.
The condemned choice is explained as preferring worldly life over the Hereafter, a direct repeated use of the section's preference.
The believers are challenged for being content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter and told its enjoyment is slight, sharpening the scale of the choice.
The Prophet must not follow one whose heart neglects God's remembrance and follows desire, connecting failed remembrance to worldly preference.
Truth is offered as a choice, but refusal leads to a surrounding fire; this gives the reminder-choice-fire sequence a concrete boundary.
The living and dead are not equal, and the Prophet cannot make those in graves hear; this boundary clarifies why the fire's neither-dead-nor-living state is anomalous.
Jonah participates in drawing lots and becomes the losing party, another concrete scene in which an allotted share is selected rather than freely preferred.
Human creation begins from a lowly fluid, opening a womb-and-measure sequence parallel to the section's fashioned embryo.
The fluid is placed in a secure lodging, identifying the womb-side containment of that formation.
It remains there until a known measure, joining gestation directly to appointed measure.
God says that He determined it and is the best determiner, closing bodily formation with divine measurement.
God pours water abundantly, beginning the cultivated-field sequence behind the section's rain and pasture.
God splits the earth open, supplying the cracked and worked ground through which the crop emerges.
Grain is made to grow in that ground, the useful produce on the cultivated side of the section's field contrast.
Fruit and pasture are among the products of the split earth, bringing crop and grazing growth together.
Those products are provision for people and their livestock, stating the benefit of the field and pasture.
The warning is called a reminder, beginning a short sequence about receiving it under divine will.
Whoever wills may remember it, placing human response beside the offered reminder.
They remember only if God wills, closely paralleling the section's qualification of remembered recitation by divine will.
The revelation is called a reminder, and whoever wills may take a way to his Lord, joining recollection, choice, and road.
Human willing is dependent on God's will, repeating the section's boundary on choice and retention.
God admits whom He wills into mercy while preparing painful punishment for wrongdoers, completing the two destinations after the chosen way.
God knows the secret and what is still more hidden, a close verbal and contextual counterpart to the hidden knowledge later named at the fire.
Moses asks his Lord to ease his task, placing the section's promised ease in the same life that is selected at the fire.
After the surah's divisions of death, reward, and fire, the command again tells the hearer to glorify the name of the mighty Lord, matching the section's framing command.
The hearer is commanded to glorify the name of the mighty Lord after revelation is affirmed as certain truth, another exact stance of name-centered glorification.
The easing passage begins with one who gives and fears, tying the receptive branch to the fear that accepts the section's reminder.
That person affirms the best promise, distinguishing the belief that precedes being eased toward ease.
God promises to ease that person toward ease, the closest repeated formulation of the section's promise of the easy way.
The opposite branch begins with one who withholds and thinks himself self-sufficient, reversing provision used in trust.
He denies the best promise, identifying the response that leads away from the easy course.
God will ease him toward hardship, an explicit reversal that reveals ease as a morally chosen destination rather than mere comfort.
The Quran is made easy for remembrance and the hearer is asked who will remember, fusing the section's promise of ease with its command to remind.
The same ease-for-remembrance formulation recurs after an earlier destroyed people, making remembrance the benefit that survives their passing.
The ease-for-remembrance refrain recurs after another warning narrative, repeating the section's offered but dividing reminder.
A fourth occurrence again makes the Quran easy for remembrance, confirming the repeated divine stance behind the section's movement.
After the hidden Hour, Moses is warned not to be diverted by one who denies it and follows desire; this supplies the bad preference that resists the concealed reckoning.
The Prophet is told not to hurry the Quran before its revelation is completed and to ask for knowledge, a direct counterpart to receiving recitation without losing it.
The Prophet is told not to move his tongue hurriedly with revelation, staging the concern about securely receiving the recited word.
God takes responsibility for the revelation's collection and recitation, closely paralleling the section's promise that the gathered word will be read and retained.
Once God recites it, the Prophet is told to follow its recitation, completing the stance of guided reception.
God increases the guided in guidance, while enduring good deeds are better in reward and return, joining guidance to what lasts.
The Quran is eased in the Prophet's tongue to give good news to the God-fearing and warn opponents, combining ease, speech, fear, and warning.
God provides from an unexpected place, fulfills His command, and has set a measure for everything, joining hidden provision to universal measure.
Whoever fears God receives ease in his affair, linking fear directly to divinely given ease.
Spending is apportioned according to provision, and God promises ease after hardship; share, provision, and ease meet in one ayah.
Unlimited provision would provoke transgression, so God sends it down by whatever measure He wills, clarifying measure as merciful apportionment.
God apportions livelihoods in worldly life and raises people in degrees, while His mercy is better than their accumulation; allotted share, height, and the better good meet explicitly.
The Prophet must turn from one who turns from remembrance and wants only worldly life, directly joining rejected reminder to preference for the lower life.
In houses God permits to be raised, His name is remembered and He is glorified morning and evening, joining height, name, remembrance, and glorification.
Trade does not distract these people from God's remembrance and establishing prayer, and they fear the coming Day; worldly business is subordinated to remembrance, prayer, and fear.
The Prophet is commanded to remember his Lord's name morning and evening, a close parallel to the section's remembered divine name.
He is told to prostrate and glorify God at night, bringing the section's prayer posture and glorification together.
When believers are reminded of God's signs, they fall in prostration and glorify their Lord, a direct non-magician parallel to reminder becoming prostration and praise.
The command to recite in the name of the Lord who created joins recitation, the divine name, and creation in one opening.
God creates the human from a clinging clot, giving the bodily scene attached to that command.
A question introduces the person who forbids God's servant, opening a concrete obstruction of the prayer response.
What he forbids is a servant praying, the direct inverse of the section's person who remembers his Lord and prays.
The forbidden servant may stand upon guidance and command piety, showing what the attempt to stop prayer actually opposes.
The Prophet is told not to obey the opponent but to prostrate and draw near, resolving the conflict through the same posture as the believing magicians.
Believers facing an enemy are told to stand firm and remember God much so that they may prosper, joining remembrance directly to falah.
Believers are commanded to bow, prostrate, worship, and do good so that they may prosper, linking the magicians' posture to the section's falah.
The believers are declared prosperous, opening a passage that immediately identifies prayer as their first trait.
The prosperous believers are humble in prayer, explicitly connecting falah to the section's prayer branch.
At the mountain encounter Moses falls unconscious, then glorifies God and repents when he revives; Mosaic revelation, height, and glorification meet in one scene.
God calls Moses in the sacred valley of Tuwa, the concise alternate setting of the same encounter reached at the fire.
God raises the heaven's canopy and proportions it, joining height to the act of fashioning.
On the exposed Day, the human remembers what he strove for, bringing remembered effort into the once-hidden reckoning.
The Hour's endpoint belongs to the Lord alone, reinforcing the section's hidden Hour as divine knowledge.
When people see the Hour, worldly duration will seem no longer than an evening or morning, a specific measure of how little the preferred near life lasts.
The gates of heaven are opened with pouring water, beginning a flood that turns descending provision into overwhelming judgment.
Springs burst from the earth and the two waters meet for a matter already decreed, joining flood, meeting, and divine measure in one ayah.
When the water overflowed, humanity's ancestors were carried in the vessel, recalling the flood as both destruction and preservation.
The flood is made a reminder to be retained by a retaining ear, directly connecting passing waters to remembered speech that is not lost.
The flood sign begins when the oven gushes, so a vessel associated with fire becomes the source of overwhelming water in a striking meeting of the section's two scenes.
The repeated Noah account again makes the oven gush as the flood begins, confirming the fire-vessel and water conjunction.

The believers bow and prostrate while seeking God's bounty, and their growth is compared to a crop that strengthens and pleases its sowers; prostration, provision, and cultivated growth meet together.
The sun and moon move by precise calculation, extending the section's divine measure into the ordered heavens.
Plants and trees prostrate, letting the pasture itself assume the posture of the believing magicians.
God raises the heaven and establishes the balance, joining height to measured order.
Everyone upon the earth passes away, stating the disappearance side of the section's debris-and-benefit contrast.
The majestic face of the Lord remains, completing the contrast with the One enduring reality.
Everything perishes except God's face, and judgment and return belong to Him, another exact formulation of what passes and what remains.
Knowledge of the Hour belongs only to the Lord; it is heavy and comes suddenly, supplying the fuller Quranic context for the Hour kept hidden at Moses' fire.
The human is created from a mixed drop as a test and given hearing and sight, joining bodily formation to moral trial.
God guides the human to the way, after which he may be grateful or ungrateful, stating the choice opened by guidance.
Chains and a blaze are prepared for the ungrateful, carrying one branch of that guided choice into fire.
People must seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting their share of the world, a boundary that corrects preference without denying the worldly portion.
Those who desire worldly life and its adornment may receive the fruits of their deeds here, defining the preferred near-life branch.
Nothing awaits that branch in the Hereafter except fire and its worldly work comes to nothing, joining bad preference to the passing of apparent benefit.
Death occurs only by God's permission at a fixed term, and whoever desires worldly or otherworldly reward receives a share; measure, choice, death, and allotted portion meet.
After a command to remember God, some people ask only for this world and consequently have no share in the Hereafter, joining remembrance, preference, and portion.
Others ask for good in both this world and the Hereafter and protection from fire, stating the prayer of the alternative branch.
Those people receive a share of what they earned, completing the passage's corrected meaning of allotment.
God creates death and life to test whose work is best, clarifying the ordered purpose behind the section's boundary between living and dying.
The people of the Garden taste no death beyond the first death and are protected from Hell, the saved reversal of being trapped in fire without death or life.
A human mistakes expanded provision and honor for proof that the Lord has honored him, exposing a false equation between worldly share and true height.
He likewise mistakes restricted provision for humiliation, defining the boundary between measured provision and divine worth.
People are told not to covet the preference God gives others; men and women each have a share of what they earn, directly joining preference to allotted share.
Abraham's station is made a place of prayer and Abraham and Ishmael are commanded to purify the House for worshippers, joining Abraham, prayer, and purification.
Abraham declares all former objects of worship enemies except the Lord of the worlds, giving his requested distance from idols a spoken form.
Abraham identifies that Lord as the One who created him and guides him, joining his page to the section's creation-and-guidance pair.
He says that God feeds him and gives him drink, adding provision to the Abrahamic confession.
Abraham says that God causes him to die and then gives him life, bringing the life-and-death boundary into the same confession.
God chose Abraham and guided him to a straight path, pairing chosenness and guidance in the other prophet named by the section's final ayah.
God chose Abraham in the world and he is righteous in the Hereafter, joining prophetic selection to the two lives.
After God fashions the human and breathes spirit into him, the angels must prostrate, joining bodily craft to prostration.
The same command recurs: once the human is fashioned and given spirit, the angels are to fall prostrate, confirming that meeting of formation and worship.
God fashions the human, breathes spirit into him, and grants hearing, sight, and hearts, a direct bodily use of the section's craft verb.
God makes earth a dwelling, raises heaven as a canopy, beautifies human forms, and provides good things, gathering height, bodily form, and provision.
Human life proceeds from dust and drop through clot, birth, maturity, old age, and an appointed term, joining formation to measured life and death.
God creates people stage after stage in the womb within three darknesses, making bodily formation a hidden divine work.
The drop is placed in a secure lodging, locating the body-forming process in the womb.
The drop is successively made clot, lump, bones, flesh, and another creation, an extended scene of the shaping developed by the section.
The human begins as a drop of emitted fluid, contributing the material stage immediately before creation and proportioning in 75:38.
God makes the fashioned human into the male and female pair, completing the bodily differentiation after 75:38.
God creates the two sexes, male and female, a bodily creation claim within the passage following the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.
That pair comes from a drop when emitted, specifying the bodily origin in the same scriptural sequence.
At the call to Friday prayer, believers must leave trade and hasten to God's remembrance; this sets worldly commerce beneath prayer before the remembrance-and-falah command in 62:10.
The devout person spends the night prostrating and standing, fears the Hereafter, hopes for mercy, and the ayah ends by distinguishing those who remember.
Those previously given knowledge fall on their faces in prostration when revelation is recited, paralleling the magicians' immediate bodily response to truth.
While prostrate they glorify their Lord and affirm His promise, joining recited revelation to glorification.
They fall down weeping and the recitation increases their humility, completing the posture of receptive remembrance.
Woe is pronounced upon some who pray, establishing that the bodily act alone does not guarantee the section's saved branch.
Those worshippers are heedless of their prayer, showing that prayer severed from remembrance reverses the section's pairing.
Hypocrites stand for prayer lazily, showing off and remembering God only a little, another precise boundary around genuine prayer and remembrance.
Prayer continues even under fear, and after safety believers must remember God for what He taught them, joining fear, prayer, teaching, and remembrance.
